periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Before-Reading Activation and Shared Reading of Section A

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Pair discussion: Republic Day Parade and bravery awards
Group discussion: qualities of a soldier

phases.description: Teacher opens with a brief think-aloud about the Republic Day Parade, inviting students to share what they know about bravery awards given on 26 January. Pairs discuss using prompts from Let us read (before-reading, p.49).

Groups of four discuss the qualities a soldier should have and what message they would share with a soldier, using the group discussion prompt from Let us read (p.49). Teacher circulates and notes key words on the board.

Teacher reads the prose aloud — Section A text (p.49–58) — with students following in their books. Teacher pauses at key moments (Operation Gulmarg, D Company's airlift, Sharma's declaration) to check comprehension with brief oral questions.
Teacher briefly recaps the main events of the battle and previews the next period's comprehension and extract work. Students note two facts they found surprising.

periods.teacher_notes: This first period anchors prior knowledge before the demanding prose; do not rush the before-reading discussion. The prose_summary notes Sharma's 'I know my men better than anyone else' declaration — use it as a hook during reading. The chronological-order task (task index 2) is reserved for the next period.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Comprehension Deep-Dive: Chronology and Extract Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Arrange battle events in chronological order
Extract 1: inference and assertion-reason questions

homework.task_brief: Extract 2: questions on Sharma's early life

phases.description: Quick recap: teacher asks two students to retell one event each from the battle. Class then works individually on the chronological-order task from Let us discuss (p.59), arranging eight events in sequence.

Teacher projects or reads Extract 1 (p.59–60) aloud. Students work in pairs on the MCQ inference item, the fill-in-the-blank, and the assertion-reason question from Let us think and reflect. Class discussion follows with teacher clarifying the decoy attack strategy mentioned in the prose.
Teacher reviews correct answers for chronology and the extract questions orally. Homework is set: read Extract 2 (p.60–61) and attempt the four questions independently before the next period.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the sequence of Sharma's airlift date (31 October) and the battle date (3 November) — reinforce this during the chronology task. Extract 2 questions on early influences are manageable as homework given the prose_summary's detail on his Kangra birth and Sandhurst training.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Listening to the Param Vir Chakra Talk and Speaking for Nation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fill blanks while listening to Param Vir Chakra talk
Group speech: how to serve the nation

phases.description: Teacher briefly reviews Extract 2 homework answers (2–3 items orally). Bridge: 'We've read about the PVC — now we'll hear about it.'

Teacher reads or plays the Param Vir Chakra listening transcript (p.98) twice. Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences from Let us listen (p.66) while listening. Answers are checked as a class.

Speaking task from Let us speak (p.66–67): groups of 4–5 use the sentence prompts to organise a short speech on serving the nation, choosing one theme (environment, health, helping others, or righteous conduct). Two groups share with the class; teacher gives brief feedback on clarity and organisation.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.98) mentions Sage Dadhichi and the Vajra design; students may need a quick visual on the board to contextualise. The speaking task connects the PVC's ideals to students' own civic roles — encourage all voices, as NCF notes some students hesitate due to socio-cultural factors.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Battlefield Idioms, Collective Nouns, and Subject-Verb Agreement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match battlefield idioms; complete sentences with idioms
Match collective nouns for armed forces; fill blanks
Subject-verb agreement: fill blanks and correct passage

homework.task_brief: Over- prefix verbs: fill blanks and make word list

phases.description: Teacher introduces the four battlefield idioms from Let us learn (p.62) — fight to the last man, foil the plan, deliver a blow, hold their ground — by reading two sentences from the prose. Students match expressions to situations in Column 2 and complete sentences A–D.

Collective nouns activity (p.62–63): teacher writes regiment, squadron, fleet, battalion on the board and elicits guesses before the matching task. Students complete both the matching and the fill-in-the-blank sentences. Brief whole-class check.

Subject-verb agreement (p.65–66): teacher explains key rules (collective nouns, neither/nor, each/one) with two examples from the prose. Students complete the ten-sentence fill-in task, then work in pairs to correct the passage. Homework: over- prefix verbs task (p.64).

periods.teacher_notes: The prose_summary uses 'D Company of the 4th Battalion' and 'squadron' — link these real examples to the collective nouns task to ground the vocabulary in context. The advice/advise noun-verb spelling task (task index 3) and over- prefix task are assigned as self-study; flag them briefly for independent practice.

periods.section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
periods.activity_title: Formal Letter of Enquiry and Exploring Gallantry Awards

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Write formal letter of enquiry to memorial incharge
Research PVC awardees and women in Indian Armed Forces

phases.description: Teacher introduces the letter of enquiry format (p.67): explains heading, salutation, body paragraphs (dates, duration, fees, guidelines), and closing. Key phrases are modelled on the board.

Students draft their formal letters of enquiry (Let us write, p.67–68) to a memorial incharge, using the layout and cues provided. Teacher circulates, giving formative feedback on format and tone. Students who finish early begin proofreading.

Beyond-the-Text project launch (Let us explore, p.68–69): teacher introduces Captain Vikram Batra's passage and assigns research groups. Groups spend 10 minutes scanning the textbook pages and making notes on gallantry awards and women's roles in the Armed Forces to share next class.
Quick share-out: one group previews a finding. Teacher previews the transition to Section B (Somebody's Mother) for the next period.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose_summary details Major Sharma's Param Vir Chakra citation — use this as a concrete reference when modelling the letter's context. The patriotic songs task (beyond_text task index 1) is noted here as a self-study pointer; students may explore it independently or as extended homework.

periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem: Before-Reading and Shared Poem Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Before-reading: helping memory, word association, ragged meaning
Arrange poem events in correct order

phases.description: Before-reading (p.70): students write two feeling-words about a time they helped someone, then work in pairs to circle and underline words for elderly vs. school student. Teacher introduces the word 'ragged' with the MCQ context from the opening lines.

Teacher reads the poem aloud (p.70–72) with expression, then students re-read silently. Teacher highlights the AABB couplet structure and points to the simile 'like a flock of sheep' and the repetition of 'somebody's mother' as named in the poem appreciation summary.

Let us discuss: students arrange the eight poem events in correct sequence (p.73) individually, then compare with a partner. Class reviews the answer together, with teacher tracing the narrative arc from the woman's wait to her closing prayer.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's AABB rhyme scheme gives it a ballad-like rhythm — read it at a steady pace so students hear the couplets. Students sometimes confuse 'the gayest laddie' with the general group of boys; clarify that only one boy pauses, as the appreciation summary notes. The fill-in task on theme, tone, and structure (task index 2) will be covered in the next period.

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices, Imagery, and Extract-Level Analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fill blanks: theme, tone, structure, rhyme scheme
Identify simile, alliteration, repetition in the poem
Reason for repetition of 'somebody's mother'; analogy

phases.description: Teacher leads the fill-in-the-blank task on theme, tone, and rhyme scheme (Let us discuss II, p.73). Students answer individually, then teacher confirms answers — central theme is kindness and empathy, tone is sympathetic and hopeful, rhyme scheme AABB.

Poetic devices (Let us discuss III, p.73): teacher elicits one example of simile, alliteration, and repetition from students before confirming the textbook examples. Imagery task (Let us discuss IV, p.73) follows — students complete two sentences about the bustling street and wintry weather imagery.

Repetition and analogy tasks (Let us discuss V–VI, p.74): students complete 'The poet repeats the phrase Somebody's mother because…' and the analogy 'The old woman: vulnerable and neglected :: The young boy: ___'. Pairs share answers; teacher highlights the poem's moral pivot as described in the appreciation summary.
Homework set: Extract 1 questions (p.74). Teacher briefly reads the extract aloud so students have the lines fresh.

periods.teacher_notes: The appreciation summary identifies alliteration ('firm and strong') specifically — use this to model how to locate alliteration before students attempt independently. Imagery task 4 and the analogy task (task indices 4 and 5) work well together as they both hinge on contrasts between the woman and the boy.

periods.activity_title: Word-Search Antonyms, Matching Poem Words, and Hand Idioms

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Match poem words to underlined phrases
Match 'hand' idioms to meanings

homework.task_brief: Word-search for antonyms of poem words

phases.description: Matching task (Let us learn, p.76): teacher reads the six words from the poem — hastened, heeded, stir, lend, piled, offered — and students match each to the underlined phrase in Column 2. Answers discussed briefly with attention to how each word is used in the poem's context.

'Hand' idioms (p.77): teacher introduces the six idioms with two example sentences, then students match idioms to meanings individually. Pairs compare and the class confirms. Teacher notes that 'lend a hand' appears in the poem itself — a direct link to the boy's act.

Homework: word-search antonyms task (p.76) for firm, meek, merry, kind, anxious, bent. Teacher also points out the analogy fill-in task (task index 3) as self-study; it can be attempted after the antonyms work.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem uses 'lend a helping hand' directly — students will likely spot this, making the idiom task feel grounded rather than abstract. The analogy fill-in (task index 3, p.77) is flagged as self-study since the period's task budget is full after the matching tasks.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Hero, Narrating Kindness, and Writing a Diary Entry

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fill blanks while listening to Rohan's news broadcast
Pair narration: incident where you helped someone
Write diary entry about helping someone in need

phases.description: Teacher reads or plays the listening transcript (p.99) about Rohan Ramchandra Bahir saving a woman from the Domri River. Students complete the five fill-in-the-blank sentences from Let us listen (p.78) on the second listening. Answers checked as a class.

Speaking (Let us speak, p.79): students work in pairs to narrate an incident where they helped someone, using cue cards (at school, at the market, in the neighbourhood, in the playground) and the sentence prompts. Each partner takes a turn. Teacher circulates and notes positive examples.

Writing (Let us write, p.80): teacher briefly recaps the diary entry format — date, salutation, narrative with feelings. Students draft their diary entries including the day's description, whom they helped, how, the person's reaction, and their own feelings. Teacher gives formative feedback during drafting.
Two students share a sentence or two from their diary. Teacher previews Section C (Verghese Kurien) for the next period, bridging the theme of service across all three sections.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task index 0 (picture-sequencing) requires the printed textbook pictures; if unavailable, substitute with the fill-in task (index 1) already selected. The poem's closing prayer — 'God be kind to the noble boy, Who is somebody's son' — can be read aloud before the writing task to set the reflective tone.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Before-Reading Communication Timeline and Shared Reading of Section C

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Before-reading: communication timeline and pair discussion
Identify facts and opinions in the letter

phases.description: Before-reading (p.82): students arrange six means of communication in a timeline individually, then discuss in pairs — reasons for change, preferred means, and social media benefits and precautions. Teacher takes brief contributions from two pairs.

Teacher reads the letter (p.82–85) aloud — Kurien's voice to grandson Siddharth — with students following. Teacher pauses at three key moments: the contrast of telephone vs. letter, the decision to stay in Anand, and the Padma Vibhushan ceremony with Siddharth.

Let us discuss (p.85–86): students work individually to classify the eight statements as fact or opinion, then compare with a partner. Teacher leads a whole-class review, distinguishing Kurien's personal reflections (opinion) from dateable events (fact).
Teacher previews Extract 1 questions for the next period and notes that the letter's theme of integrity as foundational value will anchor the next comprehension session.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose_summary notes Kurien contrasts 'ephemeral telephone communication' with the 'enduring value of written letters' — this is the entry point for the fact/opinion task. Students often classify personal convictions as facts; use the Kurien example to model the distinction carefully.

periods.section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
periods.activity_title: Synonyms, Expressions, and Dash Punctuation from Kurien's Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Replace underlined words with correct synonyms from box
Match letter expressions to meanings

homework.task_brief: Insert em dash or en dash in sentences

phases.description: Synonym task (Let us learn, p.88): teacher reads each of the six sentences aloud, then students replace the underlined word with the correct synonym from the box — essential, swift, lifelong, momentary, useful, splendid. Answers discussed, with teacher pointing back to the sentences' origin in Kurien's letter where possible.

Expressions matching (p.89): students match six expressions — in all humility, hold their heads high, to be quite honest, to the best of your ability, looked at in awe, somewhere deep down — to their meanings. Teacher highlights 'in all humility' as reflecting Kurien's own voice in the letter, per the prose_summary.

Homework: em dash and en dash insertion task (p.90). Teacher models one example of each on the board. Notes: the possessives/contractions task (index 4) and prepositional phrases task (index 5) are flagged as self-study for independent follow-up.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose_summary notes Kurien's emphasis on integrity and humility — the expression 'in all humility' directly reflects this, making it the richest item for discussion. The word-building antakshari task (index 2) is not anchored due to time constraints and is noted as a self-study pointer for motivated students.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student activates prior knowledge and reads a historical prose narrative using shared reading and comprehension discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Republic Day bravery awards, Battle of Badgam chronology, Extract 1 battlefield inference.
items.item_stem:
Read the following events from the Battle of Badgam. They are listed out of order. Arrange them in the correct sequence by numbering them 1 to 5.

(a) Major Somnath Sharma correctly identified the initial enemy attack as a decoy and called for air strikes.
(b) D Company of the 4th Battalion, Kumaon Regiment, was airlifted to Srinagar on 31 October 1947.
(c) A mortar shell killed Major Somnath Sharma instantly as he refused to withdraw.
(d) The enemy, roughly 500 strong, launched their assault on D Company at Badgam on 3 November.
(e) Despite losing their commander, Sharma's men held the position for six more hours before being overrun.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The correct sequence is: (b) 1 — (d) 2 — (a) 3 — (c) 4 — (e) 5. D Company was airlifted first; the enemy attacked on 3 November; Sharma identified the decoy and called air strikes; he was killed refusing to withdraw; his men then held on for six more hours.

items.source_lo: Student analyses a narrative poem's structure, devices, and theme using literary reading and comprehension discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: AABB couplets, simile, alliteration, repetition of 'somebody's mother', kindness and empathy theme.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about the poem 'Somebody's Mother'. Identify which statements are TRUE and which are FALSE.

1. The poem follows an AABB rhyme scheme in which every two consecutive lines rhyme with each other.
2. The line 'Came the boys like a flock of sheep' is an example of alliteration.
3. The poet repeats the phrase 'somebody's mother' to emphasise the shared humanity of every elderly person and to explain the boy's act of empathy.
4. The tone of the poem shifts from sympathetic and helpless to hopeful and warm as the boy steps forward to help the old woman.

options.text: The poem follows an AABB rhyme scheme in which every two consecutive lines rhyme with each other.
The line 'Came the boys like a flock of sheep' is an example of alliteration.
The poet repeats the phrase 'somebody's mother' to emphasise the shared humanity of every elderly person and to explain the boy's act of empathy.
The tone of the poem shifts from sympathetic and helpless to hopeful and warm as the boy steps forward to help the old woman.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. TRUE — The poem is written in couplets following an AABB rhyme scheme throughout. 2. FALSE — 'Came the boys like a flock of sheep' is a simile, not alliteration; an example of alliteration in the poem is 'firm and strong'. 3. TRUE — The repetition of 'somebody's mother' is the poem's moral pivot, reminding the reader that every elderly person is someone's loved one, which motivates the boy's compassion. 4. TRUE — The poem opens with the woman's helplessness and the crowd's indifference, then moves to hope and warmth when the boy helps her.

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student distinguishes fact from opinion and reads an informational letter using shared reading and comprehension discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Kurien's letter to Siddharth: telephone vs. letter contrast, Anand cooperative decision, fact-opinion identification.
items.item_stem:
Dr. Verghese Kurien's letter to his grandson Siddharth contains both facts and opinions. Read the four statements below, taken from or based on the letter, and classify each as FACT or OPINION. Write your answer and give a one-sentence reason for each.

1. Dr. Kurien wrote his letter from Anand, Gujarat, in 2005.
2. Speaking on the telephone gives only an immediate but fleeting joy.
3. Dr. Kurien chose to work for a small dairy cooperative in Anand instead of pursuing metallurgy or going abroad.
4. Working in Anand was the most meaningful contribution Dr. Kurien could have made.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. FACT — It states a verifiable detail (place and year) about when and where the letter was written. 2. OPINION — It reflects Kurien's personal judgement about the value of phone conversations; others may disagree. 3. FACT — It records a verifiable career decision Kurien made, documented in the letter. 4. OPINION — It expresses Kurien's personal belief about the significance of his choice; it cannot be objectively verified.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational talk and retrieves specific details by completing fill-in-the-blank items as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Param Vir Chakra talk: Wheel of the Ultimate Brave, Gallantry Medal, Savitri Khanolkar, State Emblem, Vajra.
items.item_stem:
You will listen to a talk about the Param Vir Chakra. As you listen, complete each sentence below using one or two exact words from the talk.

1. The Param Vir Chakra signifies the 'Wheel of the Ultimate ________'.
2. The award is granted for exemplary bravery in the presence of the ________.
3. The medal was designed by ________, who drew inspiration from Sage Dadhichi.
4. At the centre of the Param Vir Chakra, on a raised circle, is the ________ of India.
5. Surrounding the central emblem are four replicas of Indra's Vajra, lined with ________ flowers.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Brave 2. enemy 3. Mrs. Savitri Khanolkar 4. State Emblem 5. lotus

items.source_lo: Student listens to a news broadcast and retrieves sequential and factual details using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: News broadcast about Rohan saving a woman from the Domri River; Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 2023.
items.item_stem:
You will listen to a special news broadcast. As you listen, complete each sentence below using one to three exact words from the broadcast.

1. The woman Rohan saved had fallen into the ________ River while washing clothes.
2. Rohan leapt into the river without any ________, putting his own life at risk.
3. The onlookers who witnessed the rescue were in awe of the young boy's ________.
4. Rohan was honoured at Vigyan Bhawan with the ________ 2023 by the President of India.
5. Rohan's act proved that when it comes to saving lives, age is ________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Domri 2. moment's hesitation 3. bravery 4. Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar 5. no barrier

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student organises and delivers a short group speech on a civic theme using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Group speech on serving the nation: environment, health, helping others, righteous conduct.
items.item_stem:
Major Somnath Sharma gave his life in service to his nation. As a citizen, you too can serve your country in everyday ways. In a group of 4–5, choose ONE of the themes below and speak for 2–3 minutes about how you propose to contribute to that cause. Organise your speech with: (1) a clear opening statement of your chosen theme, (2) two or three specific actions you will take, and (3) a closing sentence about why this contribution matters to the nation.

Themes: Saving the environment / Health and well-being / Helping others / Righteous conduct

expected_elements: States the chosen civic theme clearly in the opening.
Names at least two specific, actionable steps the student will take.
Connects individual action to a broader national or community benefit.
Speaks in coherent sentences using appropriate formal register.

items.source_lo: Student narrates a personal experience of helping someone using structured pair narration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Pair narration of a helping incident using cue cards: school, market, neighbourhood, playground.
items.item_stem: In 'Somebody's Mother', the boy helps the old woman without being asked, inspired by thinking of his own mother. Work in pairs. Take turns to narrate a real or imagined incident where you helped someone in need. Use ONE of the settings from the cue cards: at school / at the market / in the neighbourhood / in the playground. Your narration should include: (1) where and when it happened, (2) who needed help and what the situation was, (3) what you did, and (4) how both you and the other person felt afterwards.

expected_elements: Identifies the setting and situation clearly using the chosen cue card.
Describes the helping action with specific details.
Expresses the feelings of both the helper and the person helped.
Narrates in a logical sequence with appropriate past-tense language.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student plans and writes a formal letter of enquiry using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Letter to memorial incharge: visit dates, tour duration, entry fees, student group guidelines.
items.item_stem: Your school wishes to organise a visit to the National War Memorial in New Delhi, where the name of Major Somnath Sharma is etched on the Honour Wall. Write a formal letter of enquiry to the In-charge of the National War Memorial. In your letter, request information about: (a) available dates for school group visits, (b) the duration of a guided tour, (c) any entry fees for student groups, and (d) guidelines your school must follow during the visit. Use a proper formal letter format with all required parts (sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject line, salutation, body, complimentary close, and signature).

expected_elements: Uses correct formal letter format with all required parts.
Addresses all four points of enquiry clearly in the body.
Maintains a formal, polite register throughout.
Writes in clear, grammatically accurate sentences of appropriate length.

items.source_lo: Student writes a reflective diary entry about a personal experience using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Diary entry about helping someone in need: situation, feelings during and after, motivation.
items.item_stem: The boy in 'Somebody's Mother' felt 'his young heart happy and well content' after helping the old woman cross the street. Write a diary entry from the perspective of the boy, describing the events of that day. Include: (1) a description of the old woman and the situation at the crossing, (2) what made you decide to help her when the others did not, (3) how you felt while guiding her and after returning to your friends, and (4) what you hope will happen for your own mother someday. Begin your entry with a suitable date and greeting, such as: 'Dear Diary, Today was a day I will not forget…'

expected_elements: Uses correct diary format with date, greeting, and first-person voice.
Describes the old woman's situation and the decision to help using details from the poem.
Reflects on feelings during and after the helping act with genuine emotion.
Connects the act to care for one's own mother, echoing the poem's theme.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary and grammar concepts from a prose context using linguistic aspects in context as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Battlefield idioms, collective nouns for armed forces, subject-verb agreement rules.
items.item_stem:
The passage about Major Somnath Sharma uses several specialised terms and expressions related to the armed forces. Complete the tasks below.

Part A — Collective nouns: Choose the correct collective noun from the box (regiment, squadron, battalion, fleet) to complete each sentence.
1. The commanding officer reviewed every soldier in the ________ before the march past.
2. A ________ of fighter jets flew in formation over the parade ground.
3. The ________ of infantry was ordered to advance at dawn.
4. The admiral commanded the entire naval ________ to set sail.

Part B — Subject-Verb Agreement: Choose the correct verb form in brackets.
5. Each of the soldiers (was / were) awarded a medal for bravery.
6. Neither the commander nor the troops (was / were) prepared for the ambush.
7. A convoy of military vehicles (passes / pass) through the town every morning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Part A: 1. regiment 2. squadron 3. battalion 4. fleet. Part B: 5. was 6. were 7. passes.

items.source_lo: Student builds vocabulary through word-matching and idiom identification using a poem's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem words hastened, heeded, stir, lend, offered; idioms with 'hand'; antonyms of firm, meek, merry.
items.item_stem: Match each word from the poem 'Somebody's Mother' in Column A with the phrase in Column B that is closest in meaning.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
hastened | (i) paid careful attention to
heeded | (ii) moved quickly without stopping
stir | (iii) came forward with willingness to give
offered | (iv) give support or assistance
lend | (v) move slightly from a resting position

items.source_section_title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream
items.source_lo: Student applies contextual vocabulary and expression-matching skills using an informational letter as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Synonyms: essential, swift, lifelong, momentary; expressions: in all humility, hold their heads high, looked at in awe.
items.item_stem:
In his letter to Siddharth, Dr. Kurien uses vivid words and expressions. Complete the two tasks below.

Part A — Replace the underlined word in each sentence with the correct synonym from the box: (essential, swift, momentary, lifelong).
1. Dr. Kurien felt a fleeting sense of pride when he saw Siddharth slip the medal around his neck.
2. His abiding commitment to the farmers of Anand shaped every decision he made.
3. Integrity, he argued, is a core value that every person must develop.
4. With today's instant means of communication, news travels across the world in seconds.

Part B — Choose the expression from the box (in all humility, hold their heads high, looked at in awe) that best replaces the underlined phrase in each sentence.
5. Dr. Kurien said, without any sense of self-importance, that his achievements belonged to many collaborators.
6. The millions of farmers who benefited from Operation Flood can be confident and proud of what they achieved.
7. Students and citizens observed Kurien with great respect and wonder for his selfless contribution.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Part A: 1. momentary 2. lifelong 3. essential 4. swift. Part B: 5. in all humility 6. hold their heads high 7. looked at in awe.

items.source_section_title: A Tale of Valour — Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam
items.source_lo: Student researches and presents information on a civic and historical theme using project work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: PVC awardees Major Sharma to Captain Vikram Batra; gallantry awards; women in Indian Armed Forces.
items.item_stem:
Major Somnath Sharma was the first recipient of the Param Vir Chakra and Captain Vikram Batra was the last among the twenty-one awardees. The section also highlights the growing role of women in the Indian Armed Forces. Complete the project below in groups of four.

Task 1 — Gallantry Awards: Research India's three highest gallantry awards — the Param Vir Chakra, the Maha Vir Chakra, and the Vir Chakra. For each award, find out: (a) what act of bravery it recognises, (b) who instituted it and when, and (c) the name of one awardee and the conflict in which they served. Prepare a brief presentation to share with the class.

Task 2 — Women in the Indian Armed Forces: Find out about the key roles women currently hold in the Indian Army, Navy, and Air Force. Identify at least one pioneering woman officer in each service. Share your findings with classmates and teacher.

expected_elements: Accurately describes the criteria and rank of each of the three gallantry awards.
Provides verified names of at least one awardee per award with correct conflict context.
Identifies specific current roles of women in at least two of the three armed services.
Presents findings clearly and shares with the class in an organised manner.
